When the designers of the test suite decided that it passes without any additional check, it is not needed to control its outputs." and "shut the fuck up about it already" (2026-10-02T15:48:05.965Z), on the coordinator's 15:40:56.635Z offer of expected-output files.

What he refused at 15:48:05 was a new kind, an interpreter `Foo.out` beside `Foo.fss` (option 2 of the 15:40:56 question), which that question itself said "works like the compiled suite's `run_out_equals`". ## P-124

**Match.** The cold reader puts the examples in the gate at zero red under walk, fixes the implementation when one fails, does not respell an example for walk and keeps no list of known failures. He chose this with "Yep. Option one." (2026-10-04T20:27:30.337Z), answering the coordinator's 20:24:58.453Z question "Should `testSpecData` join the gate?":
- option 1, join once the five red examples are green, "the target joins the gate at zero red";
- not option 2, a list of known red names;

**The cold reader's open points.**

1. **"A test that fails or varies under parallelism is written wrong".**

The team's tests that print differently on every run (random seeds, timings, hash order: the coordinator's 2026-09-29T18:09:15.658Z text, which he quoted at 19:01:43) do so "because it does not fucking matter" (2026-09-29T19:03:33.775Z).

content.content:
one instantiation for each type that the variable may stand for,
which instantiation exclusion forbids
(\secref{trait-types} and \secref{trait-decls});
the second of the three declarations below shows why.
\revision{revival-where}{This restriction is new.
The three declarations that follow were offered as legal by the
Working Draft of February 2011; they are kept as examples of what is not
allowed, each with the way to write it.}

In particular, a trait declaration may not extend other instantiations
of itself through a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
The following declaration would express that the static parameter \VAR{S}
of \VAR{C} is covariant, making \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} a subtype of
\EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} for every supertype \VAR{T} of \VAR{S};
it is not allowed:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]
%  where {S extends T, T extends Object}
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{extends} C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{S \KWD{extends} T, T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
Static parameters are invariant:
\EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} is a subtype of \EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
only if \VAR{S} and \VAR{T} are the same type.
A value of one instantiation is widened to another by a function
whose bounded static parameters state that one argument extends the other:
%trait C[\S\]
%  getter item(): S
%end
%object CItem[\S\](item: S) extends C[\S\] end
%widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\] = CItem[\T\](c.item)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait}\:C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{getter}\:\VAR{item}()\COLON S\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object}\:\TYP{CItem}\llbracket{}S\rrbracket(\VAR{item}\COLON S) \KWD{extends}\:C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\VAR{widen}\llbracket{}T, S \KWD{extends}\:T\rrbracket(c\COLON C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket)\COLON C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket = \TYP{CItem}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(c.\VAR{item})\)
\end{Fortress}
so that, where a trait \TYP{Dog} extends a trait \TYP{Animal} and \VAR{d}
is a \EXP{C\llbracket\TYP{Dog}\rrbracket},
\EXP{\VAR{widen}\llbracket\TYP{Animal}, \TYP{Dog}\rrbracket(d)} is a
\EXP{C\llbracket\TYP{Animal}\rrbracket} with the same item.
The library's covariant collections are written this way.
\revision{revival-covariance}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves,
and gave the declaration above as the way to express covariance.
The type group's later design declares variance instead with a
\KWD{covariant} modifier on a static parameter
(the team's later Types chapter, Luchangco, 2012),
which is implemented on neither the interpreter nor the compiled path;
the revival's decision record and row~404 of its gap ledger
say what is known of it.}

- If it prints a path, run the gate.
- If not, the newest gate holds. Run only the changed test files, through `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` (`tests-running.md`).

## The steps

Run these steps from the tree's root. Keep the logs of steps 2 and 4 in `tmp/gate/`, as `compileAll.txt`, `testFast.txt`, `testSystem.txt` and `testSpecData.txt`.

1. Read the Avail column of `df -h /`. Warning: deleting `/tmp/fortress*rats` can break other live runs. If the column shows less than 1 GB, delete `/tmp/fortress*rats`, `ProjectFortress/test-tmp` and `ProjectFortress/test-caches`, and read it again. If it still shows less than 500 MB, stop and report.
2. Run `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS tmp/gate && mkdir -p tmp/gate`, then `ant compileAll`.
3. If the build printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, run the library order (`build-and-caches.md`). If not, and a source of the compiler's library changed since the caches were filled, take its step in `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library". Then copy the caches twice for the ladder regression, before anything else compiles into them:

       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; mkdir -p $D/root
       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/ladder-caches
       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/pristine

4. Run `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, then `ant testSpecData`. All three must have zero failures.
5. Write the summary: `gate_summary tmp/gate tmp/gate/summary.txt`. Compare it: `gate_compare "$(last_landed_summary)" tmp/gate/summary.txt`. It prints a line for a suite with failures or errors, a suite with no tests, a suite whose count of tests fell, and a suite that is gone. Each such line makes the gate red. A count that rose prints nothing.
6. Do the atomic runs, and append their lines to the summary.
7. Do the ladder regression.

## The atomic runs
153:## Rules for every task
154-
155-- Carry out the curator's decisions as the record states them.
156-- If the record does not settle a question that your work meets, switch to exploring.
157-- Cite a source for each claim that you write: your brief, an entry of the record, or a primary source (the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output).
158-- Reproduce a behaviour before you explain it: run a command that shows it, unless your brief cites the command's output.
159-- When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause.
160-- Write the test before the fix for every edit of source code in the original tree. Add the test to the test suite and see it fail through the harness. Then make the fix and see the test pass. An edit of the specification or the documentation has no test (`references/tests-writing.md`).
161-- Assert every value that matters inside the test, with the harness's own checks (`references/tests-writing.md`), and take the suite's pass or fail as the result. Do not compare the output of a whole run of tests with a saved copy, and do not add expected-output files. The gate's comparisons, and a comparison of outputs that your brief asks for, are the exceptions (`references/gate.md`, "Comparing with an earlier run").
162-- Take the tree that you start from as passing: its suites passed before it landed. Do not run them to check that. Start with your own failing test.
163-- Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate, a test or a measurement that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it. Run it again only after the code changes. Running a new program is not a repeat.
164-- Before you investigate a defect, or edit a file of the original tree, look for its rows in the gap ledger, with the queries of `references/records.md`, "Reading the record".
165-- After your fix, run your own tests. Run a whole suite where `references/tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite", asks for it, and nowhere else.

**The measurement** (https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/fresh-jvm-commands.md)
- **Data:** 267 worker transcripts from 2026-10-08 to this morning. The workers ran 123 hours between them, 45 of those hours inside commands.
- **One-off Fortress commands, each a fresh JVM:** 913 calls, taking 7 h 51 min. That's 17.5% of the command time and 6.4% of the workers' total time.
- **The cost of starting one:**
  - a bare JVM, 0.04 s;
  - the Fortress command line with no program, 0.29 s;
  - a walk run of a one-line program, 3.0 s.
- **What a resident compiler would save:** at most 2 h 13 min, 1.8% of the workers' time, and more likely about 1%. Even if those commands cost nothing at all, the cap is 6.4%. Half their time is in 48 long calls over 100 s each, such as whole-library compiles and test batches, which is real work.
- **Where the time does go:** the test suites, builds and stages take 47.8% of the command time. The distance stage (5 h 33 min) and the count stage (4 h 07 min) are the two biggest.

So a resident compiler isn't worth building, and I won't propose it. The lever is the checker's own speed, which is rung S.

On the rules that the revival revises, it is their latest intent, which the goal is to finish. It covers the exclusion rule, as instantiation exclusion in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, and `Bottom`, which no program can write.
40:- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.
61:- P-148 **The checker's speed comes right after its correctness.** A rung that adds to the checker first makes the change correct, then, in the same rung, makes the new code fast without changing which programs the checker accepts or refuses, so that no optimization is left for after the landing. The aim is a checker that stays usable as it grows: some slowdown is fine, but new checks have made it orders of magnitude slower, enough to hold a landing. The timing is a smoke test: one run, to catch a slowdown of several times; a small difference is noise. Built in the `fortress-repo` skill (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time").

      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;
`remove F-90`; `merge F-91 into F-87`; `note F-87`, or `note F-87 correcting
TIME`, a noted block. Each may be followed by one indented provenance line of
its own:
`  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; by: WHO; note: WHY`. Blank lines and
`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,
once in a file.

check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
or `removed`; a noted block that holds an earlier line, or whose `correcting`
names no earlier block of its entry, or more than one; a pointer to no live
entry, or quoted words that do not open the target's title; with --base, an
entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now nor the earlier line of a block
in its history (pointer words refreshed by the tool aside). It reports, without failing: the entries over 600 characters, the
entries without a bold title, and the `--from` paths and the report sections
an entry cites (`PATH`, "HEADING") that do not resolve.

The reads are facts-extract.sh's: `F-87`, `F-87+` (with the entries it points
to and that point to it), `history:F-87`, and the title queries, which fall
back to the former titles in the history.
